title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: DTE lands big data center deals despite earnings miss—what it means for your electric bill tonight.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into DTE's latest moves—new data center contracts that are shaping growth even after an earnings miss, and what that could mean for rates across southeast Michigan.
That's the one that stood out to me today, Graham. DTE missed earnings targets but still landed these big deals. How does that even work?
From their quarterly slides released today, the utility is pointing to these data center contracts as a key growth driver going forward. They're expecting the new load to boost revenue over time.
But ratepayers end up paying for the infrastructure, right? Can you walk me through how that plays out historically in Michigan?

Exactly. Utilities like DTE recover costs for new transmission and generation through rate cases. We've seen this pattern before with other large industrial loads—upgrades get built, and those expenses get spread across all customers unless regulators push back.
So what's different this time with data centers? Are we talking gigawatts here, or smaller projects?

The deals announced today are significant enough that DTE is already factoring them into future grid investments. That means more power lines, substations, and potentially new generation capacity in southeast Michigan.
And that ties right into the water and farmland concerns we've heard in other parts of the state. How do these projects usually affect local resources?

Data centers need massive amounts of electricity and often cooling water. In rural areas that's led to fights over farmland conversion and aquifer strain. Here in DTE territory it's more about the electric grid, but the same principle applies—sudden demand spikes force infrastructure changes.
Who are the main players pushing these deals? Is it mostly hyperscalers like the big tech firms?

Primarily yes—large tech companies looking for reliable power near existing transmission. DTE has positioned itself as ready to serve that load, which is why the contracts are highlighted even with the earnings miss.
What happens next for ratepayers? Are we looking at immediate bill increases, or is this more long-term?

It'll play out in upcoming rate cases. DTE has already noted that data center growth is an earnings driver, which often translates to requests for higher rates or new charges to cover the buildout. Regulators will have to decide how much gets passed along.
We've seen towns pushing back with moratoriums lately. Does today's news change the pressure on local officials?
It could. If DTE is locking in more load, communities near new substations or lines might see renewed interest from developers. That often accelerates the local debates we've covered.
And the noise and buyout issues in places like Dowagiac—does that scale up with bigger DTE-backed projects?

Larger facilities tend to bring louder cooling systems and more 24/7 operations. The pattern from other states shows residents pushing for stricter sound rules or even relocation offers once the hum starts.
How many Michigan townships have already hit pause on this kind of growth?

At least a handful in the past week alone—Utica extended its ban, Chippewa County is considering a freeze, Garfield Township blocked new proposals for a year. It's becoming a common tool while they study the impacts.
What about the Senate candidates' split on this? Does DTE's news give voters more to chew on?

The Democratic primary contenders outlined different approaches on Saturday—some want utilities or tech firms to cover more of the transmission costs, others are open to spreading it across ratepayers. Primary voters now have clear contrasts on an issue that hits monthly bills.
Indiana Michigan Power made that pledge to shield residents. Is DTE under similar pressure?
Not yet publicly, but consumer groups are watching. Indiana Michigan's commitment came amid the same AI-driven demand concerns. DTE's rate cases will likely face the same questions.
Bottom line for southeast Michigan tonight—what should listeners watch for in the coming months?
Keep an eye on DTE's next filings and any new rate requests tied to these contracts. Local planning commissions will also be busy as the load growth ripples outward.
Thanks for grounding that, Graham. Let's move to quick hits.
Yesterday a teacher was arrested at a city commission meeting in the Upper Peninsula after clapping during public comments against a data center proposal.
That shows how tense these fights have gotten. Residents are worried about noise, rates, and water use—what happens when emotions run that high?
It highlights the divide between project supporters and neighbors. Similar tensions popped up in St. Clair County, where an opinion piece weighed constant humming against promised jobs.
And in Dowagiac, neighbors are suing over nonstop noise that sounds like a vacuum running. The company got fined and is now offering buyouts.
That's a direct quality-of-life hit. Utica extended its moratorium yesterday to protect power and water capacity from sudden spikes.
Chippewa County is also weighing a temporary freeze on new proposals while they study land, power, and service impacts.
Garfield Township did the same on Friday after a sloppy project filing—blocking new centers for at least a year.
On the candidate side, Indiana Michigan Power pledged on Saturday to shield ratepayers from data center costs. That's a concrete step amid the broader debate.
DTE's own preview shows data centers boosting profits, which could mean bigger bills for customers unless regulators intervene.
Now for On Deck—any meetings listeners can attend this week?
No major public hearings scheduled for tonight, but several township boards are expected to discuss data center rules later this week. We'll track those agendas and let you know.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening—stay informed on how these projects reshape Michigan.

episode_title: DTE's New Data Center Contracts: Power Bills and Grid Strain Ahead
